title: Round 4: Debug a React performance regression
description: Use a systematic approach to find and fix React performance regressions, from identifying expensive renders to optimizing state updates and list virtualization.

data.text: A feature shipped last week, and now a dashboard page feels sluggish. The user scrolls through a table of two hundred rows, and every keystroke in a filter field pauses the UI. You need to explain how you would investigate this in a React application without rewriting the whole page.

items: Re-rendering large lists because the parent passes new function references on every render
Expensive calculations running during render instead of being memoized or moved to a worker
Uncontrolled state updates that cause siblings to re-render unnecessarily
Missing keys in lists, causing React to destroy and recreate DOM nodes instead of moving them
Third-party scripts competing for main-thread time during interactions
Layout thrashing: reading layout properties (offsetWidth) inside render, forcing synchronous reflows

terms.definition: React's algorithm for comparing the new virtual DOM tree with the previous one to determine which DOM nodes to update.
Caching the result of a computation or component render so it is only recalculated when inputs change.
Rendering only the visible subset of a large list to keep DOM node count constant.
The phase where React calls your component function to calculate what the UI should look like. This should be pure and fast.
Interleaving DOM reads and writes, forcing the browser to recalculate layout repeatedly during a single frame.

data.text: React DevTools Profiler is your first tool. Record a profiling session while interacting with the slow component. Look for bars that are wider than expected, especially if a component renders even though its props did not change. That is a sign of an unstable reference or missing memoization.

data.title: Before and after memoization
data.content: A parent component creates a new handler on every render, causing the child to re-render unnecessarily:

items: Open React DevTools Profiler and record the interaction that feels slow.
Check the 'Ranked' view to see which components commit the most time.
Use the 'Why did this render?' tooltip to inspect prop changes.
Verify the fix by profiling again and confirming the render count or duration drops.
Add a performance test if the regression was caught by a test suite.

data.title: Measure before optimizing
data.text: Do not wrap everything in React.memo or useMemo on day one. Each memoization adds complexity and memory overhead. Measure, find the hot path, then optimize surgically. Interviewers care more about your process than your guess.

React 19 introduces the React Compiler, which automatically memoizes components and hooks at build time. It eliminates many manual useMemo and useCallback calls by understanding your component's data flow. However, the compiler cannot fix expensive logic inside render functions or layout thrashing. Use it as a force multiplier, not a replacement for profiling.

items: Use useMemo for expensive calculations that depend on specific dependencies, not for simple arithmetic.
Colocate state so only the branch that needs it subscribes to updates.
Use React.startTransition for non-urgent state updates like filtering or pagination.
Implement list virtualization with react-window or react-virtuoso when lists exceed fifty items.
Avoid inline object and array literals in JSX props; extract them outside the component or memoize them.
Move heavy computations to Web Workers when they block the main thread for more than 50ms.

data.title: When to use each optimization technique

cards.title: useMemo / useCallback
cards.description: Cache values and functions between renders.
pros: Stabilizes object references for useEffect dependencies
cons: Can mask underlying state design problems

cards.title: State colocation
cards.description: Move state down to the component that actually uses it.

cards.title: Virtualization
cards.description: Render only the visible rows of a large list.
pros: Constant DOM size regardless of data length

cards.title: React Compiler (React 19)
cards.description: Build-time automatic memoization of components and hooks.
pros: Zero manual useMemo/useCallback for most cases
cons: Cannot optimize imperative code or side effects

data.caption: React render cycle showing where memoization and virtualization intervene
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[User Input] --> B[State Update]
    B --> C{Component needs render?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Render Function]
    D --> E{Expensive calc?}
    E -->|Yes| F[useMemo cache hit/miss]
    E -->|No| G[Virtual DOM diff]
    F --> G
    G --> H{List > 50 items?}
    H -->|Yes| I[Virtualized window]
    H -->|No| J[Full DOM commit]
    I --> J
    J --> K[Paint & Layout]

data.title: Profile a real React app
data.description: Open any React application in your portfolio or a public repo. Use React DevTools Profiler to find the top three most expensive renders. Write down the root cause for each and propose a fix without changing any code.
steps: Open the Profiler tab and start recording
Interact with the slowest part of the app
Stop recording and analyze the flamegraph
Document the component name, render time, and suspected cause
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to identify unnecessary re-renders, missing memoization, and expensive calculations purely from profiling data.

data.title: Summary
points: Profile with React DevTools before changing code
Look for unnecessary re-renders and expensive calculations
Use stable references and virtualization for large lists
Verify the fix with the same profiler session
Prefer state colocation and startTransition over blanket memoization
data.takeaway: A good answer shows that you rely on data and tooling, not instinct, and that you understand the cost of premature optimization.
